title: The pentagon gap
hook: Squares and hexagons tile a floor. The neat, regular pentagon looks like it should too.

knows: angles in degrees; a full turn is 360
doesNotKnow: the 360-degree test for whether a shape can tile around a point

misconception: If a shape is regular and neat, it must be able to tile a floor.
objective: The learner can explain that tiles meeting at a point must fill exactly 360 degrees, so a regular polygon tiles only if its corner divides 360: triangles, squares and hexagons, not pentagons.

claims.text: The corner of a regular n-sided polygon is (n - 2) x 180 / n degrees: 60 for a triangle, 90 for a square, 108 for a pentagon, 120 for a hexagon.
claims.source: Angle sum of an n-gon is (n - 2) x 180 (split into n - 2 triangles); divided equally among n corners. Values recomputed with node from the same corner() function the stage draws with.

claims.text: Three regular pentagons around a point fill 324 degrees and leave a 36 degree gap; a fourth would overlap by 72 degrees.
claims.source: 3 x 108 = 324, 360 - 324 = 36, 4 x 108 - 360 = 72; recomputed with node from the stage's fits() and corner().

claims.text: Six triangles (6 x 60), four squares (4 x 90) and three hexagons (3 x 120) each fill exactly 360 degrees around a point.
claims.source: Arithmetic, recomputed with node from the stage's functions.

claims.text: Where tile corners meet at a point they must fill exactly 360 degrees; corners meeting against another tile's straight edge must fill 180 degrees.
claims.source: A full turn around a point is 360 degrees; a straight edge occupies 180 of it. No gaps or overlaps means the angles at the point sum exactly.

claims.text: Regular pentagons cannot tile the plane in any arrangement; among regular polygons only triangles, squares and hexagons tile on their own.
claims.source: Grunbaum and Shephard, Tilings and Patterns (1987), section 2.1; follows from 108 dividing neither 360 nor 180.

recall.question: A regular octagon's corner is 135 degrees. Can regular octagons alone cover a floor with no gaps?
options: No: 135 does not go into 360 a whole number of times
Yes, if you rotate some of them
recall.why: Tiles meeting at a point must fill 360 degrees exactly. Two octagons make 270, three make 405: a gap or an overlap, whichever way you turn them.
